adversarial_test_results.prompt: After months of saving and planning, our small group of friends finally set out on a slow journey along the coast, with no fixed schedule and only a rough map marked with harbors, lighthouses, and quiet fishing villages. We traveled by train for the first stretch, watching green hills roll past the windows while vendors walked the aisles selling tea, bread, and roasted nuts. At the border town we switched to a battered bus that rattled through mountain passes, past waterfalls and terraced fields where farmers waved as we passed. Our driver, an elderly man with endless stories, stopped at every viewpoint and insisted we taste the local cheese, honey, and dark coffee. Nights were spent in family guesthouses with creaking stairs, bright quilts, and balconies facing the sea, where we fell asleep to the sound of waves and distant music from the harbor taverns. In one harbor we joined fishermen at dawn, hauling nets heavy with silver fish while gulls circled overhead and children laughed on the pier, and the captain explained how the tides decide the working day. Another morning we hiked a cliff path lined with wildflowers, pines bent by the wind, and sudden gaps revealing the blue water far below, stopping often to rest our legs and share oranges. We mailed postcards from tiny shops, learned a few words of the local dialect, burned our shoulders in the afternoon sun, and argued happily about which cove had the clearest water for swimming. The market days were the best part, with stalls piled high with figs, olives, woven baskets, copper pots, and bright scarves, while musicians played drums and flutes in the square and cooks fried flatbread over open flames. We joined a cooking lesson in a courtyard kitchen, grinding spices, rolling dough, and tasting soup straight from the pot as the teacher corrected our technique with great patience. Rain caught us once on an exposed ridge, so we sheltered in a stone hut with shepherds, drank hot tea, and waited out the storm listening to thunder roll across the valley. By the final week the group had fallen into an easy rhythm of early starts, long walks, shared meals, and late talks under the stars about work, family, and plans for next spring. The local festival closed our trip with dancing, lanterns, paper boats set afloat on the river, and a night market that stayed open until sunrise. The whole route drew twice as many visitors compared with last year.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Long travel narrative placing the licensed 'compared with' construction hundreds of tokens deep, testing that retrospective licensing survives long contexts, so the hypothesis predicts fire.
